why: A product cannot claim to cure, treat or heal a medical condition. This is the fastest route to a rejection and an account restriction.
fix: Move to benefit language with a hedge: "may support restful sleep" instead of "cures insomnia".

why: Same rule as above, without naming the condition.
fix: Name what the product does, not what it fixes: "supports joint comfort".

why: Guaranteed outcomes are not allowed in health and weight claims, and they read as an absolute promise.
fix: Remove the guarantee. Use "designed to" or "may help".

why: Promising a specific outcome inside a specific window is a clickbait and unreliable-claims violation.
fix: Drop the timeline, or state it as an average with a qualifier.

why: A specific amount of weight loss is a guaranteed outcome and gets rejected on health products.
fix: Talk about the mechanism, not the number: "supports a calorie deficit".

why: Instant results are not credible and fall under exaggerated claims.
fix: Describe the normal experience: "most people notice a difference in the first month".

why: Meta bans copy that asserts or implies something about the viewer health or body. This is their own example of a rejected line.
fix: Speak about the product, not the reader: "New sleep support formula" instead of "Struggling to sleep?".

why: Negative statements about a person body are explicitly prohibited.
fix: Describe the goal neutrally: "a flatter midsection".

why: Supplements are not FDA approved, and "clinically proven" needs a citation you probably cannot show.
fix: Use "made in an FDA registered facility" or "clinically studied ingredient" only with a source.

why: Claims that the product works without diet or exercise are prohibited in weight management.
fix: Remove the promise and describe the product routine.

why: Before and after is allowed only for cosmetics shown to adults, and never for supplements. Risky.
fix: Drop the side by side, or use a single adult-only lifestyle image.

why: Sensational language falls under exaggerated claims and often triggers manual review.
fix: Replace with a plain functional benefit.

why: Unqualified superlatives invite a substantiation request.
fix: Say what it is better at, with a number.

why: Urgency is allowed but repeated scarcity in health ads raises scrutiny.
fix: Keep one honest deadline, remove the rest.

why: Naming a condition anywhere in the copy invites a deeper review, even when the sentence is neutral.
fix: Use the symptom or the benefit instead of the diagnosis.

pattern: (i lost|my results|it worked for me|changed my life)
why: Personal results need a clear disclaimer and must be plausible.
fix: Add "results vary" and keep the claim modest.

why: Refunds are fine, but pairing them with results reads as a guarantee.
fix: State the refund policy separately from the outcome.

why: Health and weight products must be targeted to 18 and over.
fix: Set the minimum age to 18+ in the ad set.

why: Long headlines get truncated on most placements.
fix: Keep the headline under 40 characters.

why: Specific income promises are a financial-services violation and a classic affiliate rejection.
fix: Describe the offer, not the earnings.

pattern: (get rich|passive income guaranteed|financial freedom in|double your money)
why: Guaranteed wealth claims are prohibited in finance ads.
fix: Remove the outcome promise.

pattern: (erase your debt|wipe out debt|debt free in \d+|eliminate credit card debt)
why: Debt relief carries strict rules and is often restricted outright.
fix: Say "debt consolidation options" and route to a licensed provider.

why: Prescription brands cannot be used to sell a supplement, and comparison claims get rejected instantly.
fix: Describe the category, never the brand.

why: Implying prescription equivalence is a hard block.
fix: Remove the comparison entirely.

pattern: (no side effects|zero side effects|100% safe|completely safe)
why: Absolute safety claims cannot be substantiated and invite a review.
fix: Use "generally well tolerated" with a consultation note.

why: Detox and parasite claims are a known scam pattern and get extra scrutiny.
fix: Speak to the ingredient and the routine.

pattern: (reverse aging|turn back the clock|age backwards|anti[- ]aging miracle)
why: Reversing ageing is an unsubstantiated outcome claim.
fix: Say "supports skin hydration" instead.

why: Hormone claims need substantiation and often trip health review.
fix: Use "supports healthy hormone levels" only with evidence.

why: Shouting copy reads as low quality and lowers delivery even when it passes review.
fix: Use sentence case.

why: Three or more exclamation marks is the classic spam signal.
fix: Keep one.

why: Generic CTAs underperform and add no information.
fix: Name the action: "See the ingredient list".

why: Copy that asserts something about the viewer health or body is prohibited, even as a question.
fix: Talk about the product, not the reader.

why: Promising to erase debt is a restricted financial claim.
fix: Say debt consolidation options and route to a licensed provider.

why: Talking about reducing a symptom or inflammation reads as treating a medical condition, not supporting normal function.
fix: Say what the product supports: "supports joint comfort and mobility".

pattern: (i am a|as a)\s+(registered\s+)?(dietitian|dietician|nutritionist|pharmacist|nurse|doctor|physician)|i recommend this supplement to my (clients|patients)
why: Professional authority plus a health outcome is one of the most common rejection patterns.
fix: Drop the credential and the recommendation, describe the formula instead.

why: Implying a product prevents illness is a disease claim.
fix: Use "supports your immune system" with no outcome promise.

why: A specific percentage improvement needs heavy substantiation and is usually treated as misleading.
fix: Remove the number and describe the mechanism.

why: This talks directly to the reader about their body, which the personal attributes rule forbids.
fix: Lead with the product: "A daily probiotic built to support digestive comfort".

pattern: (do you suffer from|do you have|are you living with|living with)\s+(\w+\s+){0,2}(ed|erectile|bloating|anxiety|depression|pain|insomnia|acne|hair loss|fatigue)
why: A question that presumes a condition is the textbook personal attributes rejection.
fix: Describe the service: "Prescription treatment options, reviewed online".

why: Healing or fixing a body part is a treatment claim.
fix: Use "supports a healthy gut microbiome".

why: A day-by-day transformation or a clothing-size drop is a before and after claim, which is near-automatic rejection in supplements.
fix: Show the routine, not the transformation.

why: Specific percentage outcomes are unsubstantiated performance promises.
fix: Remove the number.

why: Efficacy claims for a condition are rejected even in telehealth ads. Sell access to care, not the outcome.
fix: Use access language: "get a prescription reviewed by a licensed clinician".

pattern: (watch the (pounds|fat) melt|pounds melt away|fat melts off)
why: Implies the product does the work alone, which weight management rules prohibit.
fix: Describe the routine the product fits into.

why: Comparisons that disparage a medicine or clinic carry a high substantiation bar and often trigger review.
fix: Compare on convenience, not on efficacy or price.

pattern: (hate what you see|disgusted by|ashamed of)\s+(in the mirror|your body|your reflection)
why: Statements of inferiority about appearance are prohibited.
fix: Focus on what the product does, not how the reader looks.
